interactions: Atracurium with pyridostigmine: cholinesterase inhibitors antagonise non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade and make the response unpredictable; reversal with neostigmine adds to the cholinergic load (bradycardia, bronchorrhoea).
Atracurium with prednisolone (long-term corticosteroid): prolonged neuromuscular blocker exposure with corticosteroids is associated with critical illness myopathy and prolonged weakness.
Mycophenolate mofetil: no clinically relevant interaction with atracurium.
warnings: Myasthenia gravis: increased and prolonged sensitivity to non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers. Use a reduced dose (often a fraction of the standard dose), titrate to quantitative train-of-four monitoring, and confirm recovery before assessing spontaneous breathing.

Midazolam and other sedatives depress respiratory drive; their effect must have worn off before respiratory muscle testing.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Vital capacity 0.9 L (12.9 mL/kg), MIP -16 cmH2O and MEP 28 cmH2O, a 68% fall in vital capacity since admission, with a failed spontaneous breathing trial: neuromuscular respiratory failure.
action_criteria.label: Measure vital capacity and mouth pressures at the bedside
action_criteria.rationale: The question at the neurology consult is whether the respiratory failure is neuromuscular. Vital capacity and mouth pressures measured off sedation, against the admission values, answer it and set the weaning baseline (20/30/40 rule, Lawn 2001; Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Neutrophil leukocytosis with raised CRP; normal potassium, magnesium, phosphate and renal function; hypercapnic acidosis on the pre-intubation gas.
action_criteria.label: Order blood count, electrolytes with magnesium and phosphate, CRP and blood gas
action_criteria.rationale: A crisis needs its precipitants and aggravating factors checked: infection, hypokalaemia, hypermagnesaemia or hypophosphataemia, renal function before IVIG, and the blood gas that shows hypoventilation rather than isolated hypoxaemia (Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right upper lobe apical segment collapse with aspirated contrast; endotracheal tube in position.
action_criteria.label: Order a chest radiograph
action_criteria.rationale: After an observed aspiration and intubation, the chest radiograph confirms tube position and shows the extent of the aspiration, the precipitant of this crisis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Neutrophils with mixed oropharyngeal flora, no predominant pathogen.
action_criteria.label: Send an endotracheal aspirate for Gram stain and culture
action_criteria.rationale: Infection is the commonest crisis precipitant and his two earlier crises were infective; a lower respiratory sample guides the choice of an MG-safe antibiotic if aspiration pneumonia develops.

action_criteria.rationale: He had a thymectomy for hyperplasia 18 months ago and this crisis has an explained precipitant, so thymic re-imaging is not needed now; a CT is reasonable later in refractory disease to look for residual thymic tissue.

action_criteria.rationale: He was intubated with a standard dose of atracurium while taking pyridostigmine and prednisolone; residual block must be excluded before respiratory testing and weaning, and any further dose reduced.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not extubate before bulbar function, cough, vital capacity and inspiratory pressure have objectively recovered.
Do not attribute the respiratory failure to aspiration pneumonitis alone without measuring respiratory muscle strength.
required_recommendations: Continue ICU care with mechanical ventilation; extubate only when bulbar function and cough have recovered and vital capacity and inspiratory pressure have clearly improved on serial bedside measurements.
Start plasma exchange (5 exchanges over about 10 days) or IVIG 2 g/kg over 2 to 5 days without delay.
Hold pyridostigmine while he is intubated to limit secretions, and restart at a low dose as weaning begins.

Continue prednisolone without interruption (long-term steroid, adrenal suppression) and increase the dose while he is ventilated, so that any steroid-induced worsening occurs under ventilatory support.
Treat aspiration pneumonia, if it develops or is suspected, with an MG-safe antibiotic such as ceftriaxone or piperacillin-tazobactam, guided by the aspirate culture.
Keep him nil by mouth with nasogastric feeding, and obtain a speech and language therapy swallow assessment before any oral intake.

After the crisis, escalate maintenance immunotherapy: raise mycophenolate to a therapeutic dose (about 1000 mg twice daily) with the prednisolone; if MG stays uncontrolled despite adequate doses and duration (refractory, Sanders 2016), consider a complement inhibitor (with meningococcal vaccination; Narayanaswami 2021), rituximab or an FcRn antagonist.

results.finding: International consensus guidance: IVIG and plasma exchange are effective short-term treatments for myasthenic crisis and impending crisis; plasma exchange may act faster. Drugs known to worsen myasthenia should be avoided or used with caution. Eculizumab is an option for refractory AChR-antibody-positive generalized MG, and rituximab may be considered when initial immunotherapy fails.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: In neuromuscular respiratory failure (Guillain-Barre syndrome cohort), vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, maximal inspiratory pressure weaker than -30 cmH2O, maximal expiratory pressure below 40 cmH2O or a fall in vital capacity of more than 30% predicted progression to mechanical ventilation.
results.source: Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001;58:893-898

myasthenic crisis management.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016, update Narayanaswami 2021) supports IVIG or plasma exchange for myasthenic crisis, avoidance of drugs that worsen neuromuscular transmission, and escalation to newer agents in refractory AChR-positive disease. Serial vital capacity and mouth pressures identify impending neuromuscular respiratory failure (Lawn 2001).

patient.history_present_illness:
A 50-year-old South Asian man with a 2-year history of acetylcholine receptor antibody–positive generalized myasthenia gravis was admitted to the hospital for evaluation of progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids over the past 3 months. He had undergone video-assisted thymectomy 18 months ago (pathology: thymic hyperplasia) and had experienced two prior episodes of respiratory decompensation requiring mechanical ventilation, both precipitated by upper respiratory infections. His baseline daily medications included pyridostigmine 60 mg every 6 hours, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, and prednisolone 10 mg daily. At admission, he reported swallowing difficulty primarily with liquids causing coughing and choking spells, but no diplopia, ptosis, or limb weakness. Bedside spirometry and mouth pressures were recorded on arrival, and he was not breathless. He appeared alert and well-oriented with 5/5 limb strength bilaterally and intact gag reflex.

The gastroenterology team arranged an upper gastrointestinal fluoroscopic contrast study to characterize the degree of swallowing dysfunction. Under fluoroscopic guidance, approximately 8 mL of iohexol contrast agent was administered orally. Aspiration of contrast into the right main bronchus was immediately observed, and the study was aborted. The patient was transferred to the emergency unit on high-flow oxygen. Initial oxygen saturation was maintained above 92%, but over the ensuing 45 minutes his respiratory rate declined from 22 to 10 breaths per minute and he appeared paradoxically less distressed despite declining saturations to 87%. Nebulized salbutamol and a single intravenous dose of metronidazole 500 mg were administered without benefit. The clinical picture was attributed to aspiration pneumonitis, and the patient was intubated using IV midazolam and atracurium. A post-intubation chest radiograph was obtained. Upon ICU admission, the neurology team was consulted to reassess for possible neuromuscular contribution to the respiratory decompensation.
